content: Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) is the leading cause of maternal mortality globally. The majority of deaths related to PPH occur in low-resource settings where effective prevention and treatment methods, such as oxytocin, are often unavailable. This is primarily because many births take place at home or in community settings far from healthcare facilities. Most of the evidence supporting the effectiveness of oxytocin comes from hospital settings in high-income countries, where its administration and monitoring require well-organized care. To address this gap, simpler methods for administering oxytocin have been developed for use in resource-poor settings. However, the effectiveness of these methods has not been systematically reviewed. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of oxytocin administered in non-facility birth settings during the third stage of labor to prevent PPH. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register, the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, and ClinicalTrials.gov, as of November 12, 2015. They also reviewed reference lists of relevant reports. The inclusion criteria encompassed all published, unpublished, or ongoing randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing oxytocin administration with no intervention or standard care in non-facility birth settings. However, no quasi-randomized controlled trials or randomized controlled trials published only in abstract form were identified. Cross-over trials were excluded. The review included one cluster-randomized trial conducted in four rural districts in Ghana. In this trial, 28 community health officers (CHOs) were assigned to the intervention group, serving 2,404 potentially eligible pregnant women, while 26 CHOs were assigned to the control group, serving 3,515 potentially eligible pregnant women. The trial was assessed as having a high risk of bias. In the intervention group, CHOs administered a 10 IU injection of oxytocin into the thigh one minute after birth using a prefilled, auto-disposable syringe. In the control group, CHOs did not provide this prophylactic injection. Importantly, CHOs in both groups had no midwifery skills and did not manage the births. Their other activities, such as outcome measurement, data collection, and early treatment or referral when necessary, were identical across both groups. The results showed that only one of nine cases of severe PPH (defined as blood loss ≥ 1000 mL) occurred in the oxytocin group. However, the effect estimate for this outcome was highly imprecise, and it remains uncertain whether the intervention effectively prevents severe PPH (risk ratio [RR] 0.16, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.02 to 1.30; 1,570 women; very low-quality evidence). Similarly, due to the absence of cases of severe maternal morbidity (e.g., uterine rupture) and maternal deaths, it was not possible to estimate the effects of the intervention on these outcomes (both very low-quality evidence). Oxytocin administration was associated with a reduction in the incidence of PPH (defined as blood loss > 500 mL) in both unadjusted (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.81; 1,569 women) and adjusted analyses (RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.90; 1,174 women; both low-quality evidence). There was little to no difference between the oxytocin and control groups in terms of maternal transfer or referral to a healthcare facility (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.34 to 1.56; 1,586 women; low-quality evidence), stillbirths (RR 1.27, 95% CI 0.67 to 2.40; 2,006 infants; low-quality evidence), or early infant deaths (0 to 3 days) (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.35 to 3.07; 1,969 infants; low-quality evidence). No cases of needle-stick injury, maternal adverse events, or unanticipated harmful events were reported. Additionally, there were no instances of oxytocin use during labor. The study did not report data on several secondary outcomes, including manual removal of the placenta, maternal anemia, neonatal death within 28 days, neonatal transfer to a health facility for advanced care, breastfeeding rates, or satisfaction with the intervention from the perspective of women or providers. The authors concluded that it is uncertain whether oxytocin administered by CHOs in non-facility settings reduces the incidence of severe PPH (≥ 1000 mL), severe maternal morbidity, or maternal deaths. However, the intervention likely reduces the incidence of PPH (> 500 mL). The quality of the included trial was limited due to risks of attrition and recruitment biases, as well as baseline imbalances in birth weight. The trial was also underpowered to detect differences in primary outcomes, such as severe PPH, which are critical for determining the intervention's applicability in other settings. The extreme conditions under which the intervention was implemented, the limited role of CHOs in the trial, and the lack of power to detect effects on primary outcomes further limit the generalizability of the findings. The authors emphasized the urgent need for well-designed and adequately powered randomized controlled trials to assess the effects of oxytocin delivered via prefilled injection devices or other innovative delivery systems (e.g., spray-dried ultrafine formulations) on severe PPH. Future studies should also evaluate potential adverse events and the acceptability of the intervention among mothers and community stakeholders.
